summary: The National Parks and Conservation Association, through its Administrative Assistant for Wildlife John W. Grandy IV, argues that the draft EIS inadequately discusses alternatives and fails to evaluate areas like National Parks individually according to their legal status and primary purposes. NPCA contends that the multiple-use concept has never applied to national park areas, and that proper analysis would demonstrate that off-road vehicles should be prohibited on natural areas of the National Park System. They call for cost-benefit analyses specific to each area classification to satisfy NEPA requirements.

statement.text:
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Enclosed please find five (5) copies of my comments on the Draft Environmental Impact Statement for Proposed Implementation of Executive Order 11644, Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public Lands.
The National Parks and Conservation Association hopes they will prove useful to you.
Sincerely,
John W. Grandy, IV, Ph.D. Administrative Assistant, Wildlife

1701 Eighteenth St., N.W., Washington, D. C. 20000 Tel: (202) 265-2717
COMMENTS TO THE U.S. DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR ON THE DRAFT ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STATEMENT FOR PROPOSED IMPLEMENTATION OF EXECUTIVE ORDER 11644, PERTAINING TO USE OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES ON PUBLIC LANDS.
JULY 7, 1972
My name is John W. Grandy, IV. I am Administrative Assistant for Wildlife at the National Parks and Conservation Association.

I appreciate the invitation of this Committee to submit the views of the NPCA on this important matter.
The National Parks and Conservation Association is the leading conservation organization concerned primarily with the protection of the National Park System, but also with other major environmental and conservation subjects such as wildlife and forestry.
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the draft environmental impact statement pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands.
while the statement seems adequate in most places, alternatives to the proposed actions are insufficiently discussed.

The Secretary's memorandum (Page 3, paragraphs (a)(4) and (a)(5))
gives criteria for use of vehicles by area classifications such
as wilderness. The impact statement, however, considers all
areas as a group when considering alternatives.
27 Costs and benefits of the vehicle use pattern assigned, and alternative patterns, should be considered with reference to each area for which regulations (guidelines) are considered in (a)(4)

and (a)(5).
By adequately evaluating areas such as National Parks in relation to their legal status, their primary purposes, and all alternative sets of vehicle regulations, we believe that you will satisfy the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act. In addition, analyses will likely bring clearly to focus the extent of prohibitive regulations necessary on recreation areas, natural areas, or historic areas of the National Parks; wildlife refuges; and Bureau of Land Management lands.
The concept of multiple-use, cited as the major rationale for not closing all Interior lands to ORV use (Page 29 of draft, statement), has never been applied to national park areas either by the Congress or the adminstering agencies. Many of the recreational pursuits provided on other public lands are thus excluded from the parks. Hence, we at NPCA are certain that analyses such as we suggested will indicate that off-road vehicles should be prohibited on natural areas of the National Park System.
Again, we thank you for this opportunity to present our views and we look forward to effective regulations for individual areas published in the Federal Register.
27
Respectfully submitted,
John W. Grandy, IV, Ph.D.
